analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from lobbying Congress for life, instead of one or two years.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have made the lobbying ban on former members of Congress permanent, was introduced in March 2021 and never received a vote; it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law now bars former senators from lobbying Congress for two years and former House members for one year. This bill would have made that ban permanent — a former senator, representative, or elected officer could never return to lobby their former colleagues. Violations would carry criminal penalties. The bill was read twice in the Senate and sent to the Judiciary Committee on the same day it was introduced, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want lawmakers to make decisions based on public interest rather than future job prospects. A lifetime lobbying ban would reduce the incentive for sitting members to court industries that could hire them after they leave office, and would close one route by which former lawmakers cash in on their connections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Citizens skeptical of the revolving door

how_it_helps.text: Makes the post-employment lobbying ban permanent for former senators (currently two years), former House members (currently one year), and former elected officers of Congress (currently one year).
Applies criminal penalties under section 216 of title 18 to any former member or elected officer who knowingly lobbies Congress on behalf of someone else.
Applies to anyone who leaves office on or after the bill's enactment, so the new ban would govern all future former members.

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress and elected officers who would lose access to a lucrative post-congressional career in lobbying, along with lobbying firms and industry clients who currently hire former lawmakers for their connections on Capitol Hill.

drawbacks.text: A lifetime ban may face constitutional challenge on First Amendment grounds, since courts have struck down or limited restrictions on lobbying activity as speech and petition rights; a permanent, criminal ban is far broader than the existing one-to-two-year cooling-off periods.

The prohibition covers any lobbying contact with Congress but does not restrict other forms of post-office influence, such as advising clients informally or working in the executive branch revolving door, so its practical effect may be narrower than it appears.
It could make it harder for former members with genuine policy expertise to contribute to public debates through channels that involve contacting Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — reducing the incentive for sitting lawmakers to favor industries that might hire them later — is real and goes to public trust in government. The costs fall almost entirely on former lawmakers and the lobbying industry, which is precisely the point of the bill. The main legitimate concern is durability: a lifetime criminal ban on petitioning Congress raises First Amendment questions that courts could weigh, and it does nothing about the executive-branch revolving door. Still, compared with the current one-to-two-year bans, the trade-off favors the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on March 2, 2021, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Braun introduced the BLAST Act on March 2, 2021, for himself and Sen. Rick Scott of Florida.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced.
The bill's only listed cosponsor was one Republican senator.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress and the lobbying firms that hire them keep the current revolving door: a one-to-two-year cooling-off period followed by unrestricted lobbying. Sitting senators, whose future earning power depends on that door staying open, also benefited from the bill's quiet death.

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban former members from lobbying Congress.

for.name: Sen. Rick Scott
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in the committee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate leadership of both parties
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had Republican sponsorship and a single Republican cosponsor, but no floor votes were ever held, so no party-line split was ever tested.

industries.note: Firms that hire former members for their access to Capitol Hill would lose their most valuable recruiting pool. The bill's death keeps that talent pipeline open.

Ex-lawmakers would be barred from a career path where former senators and representatives routinely earn far more than their congressional salaries. The bill's death preserves that earnings opportunity.

industries.industry: Industries that lobby Congress (finance, pharmaceuticals, defense, and others)
industries.note: Any group whose policy goals depend on access to former members with built-in relationships keeps the current system, where a one-to-two-year wait unlocks direct lobbying by former colleagues.
